title: Inverting Miller integrator (R-C feedback around a self-biased gain stage)
description: Design an inverting (Miller) integrator -- a series input resistor into the summing node, an integrating capacitor from the output back to that node, wrapped around an inverting gain stage -- with a unity-gain frequency of about 1 kHz. Across the full sky130-style tt/ss/ff process corner, 1.62-1.98 V supply, and -40..125 C temperature matrix, the small-signal response must measure -2..+2 dB at 1 kHz, at least +15 dB at 100 Hz, and must fall by 18-22 dB over the 1 kHz -> 10 kHz decade. The three criteria are deliberately redundant: a passive R-C low-pass also rolls off at one decade per decade but can never amplify, and a plain gain stage with no feedback capacitor amplifies but never rolls off -- only an active integrator satisfies all three at once.

target_specs.corners: sky130-style tt/ss/ff process x 1.62-1.98V supply x -40..125C

reference.notes: The decade-slope criterion is a derived measurement (`.meas ac ... param='gain_1khz_db-gain_10khz_db'`), so `gain_10khz_db` is declared without limits purely as its input -- reported, never failing on its own. A large drain-to-gate feedback resistor doubles as the DC self-bias path and as the lossy-integrator pole (~10 Hz, two decades below the measured band). Generic (non-PDK) NMOS model stands in for sky130 devices; see README.md's 'Known limitation' note.

source.citation: The inverting R-C integrator is a standard analog IC design course topic; framed here in the style of AnalogCoder's (Lai et al., AAAI 2025, arXiv 2405.14918) medium-tier task set, not reproduced from that repo (unlicensed).
